source_refs.note: Gas Laws: a main subheading of 6.1 Assumptions of the kinetic theory of gases, its own page (owner 2026-11-04); PDF 119-119.

blocks.text: There are some variables (state functions) that describe quantity of gas which includes pressure, volume, and temperature (P, V, and T) with change in one variable, the second variable changes while the third is kept constant. The laws that relate these variables mutually for an ideal gas are termed as gas laws.

This law was introduced by Robert Boyle in 1662, and it provides a relationship between pressure and volume of a gas at constant temperature. It is sated that for a fixed mass of an ideal gas, the pressure P exerted by a gas varies inversely with volume V occupied by the gas at constant temperature.
Boyle's law is shown graphically in Fig. 6.1.

blocks.alt: A graph of pressure P (vertical axis) against volume V (horizontal axis), origin 0. A magenta curve falls steeply from the point (P1, V1) near the top and flattens out towards the point (P2, V2) at the right.
blocks.caption: Figure 6.1: Boyle's law shown graphically (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 6.1).

blocks.text: Charles' law relates volume and temperature of an ideal gas for a fixed mass at constant pressure. This law was formulated in 1870 by a French Physicist Jacques Charles. It is stated that the volume of given mass of gas at constant pressure is directly proportional to the absolute temperature.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Jacques Charles (1746–1823) found this law in about 1787 (Gay-Lussac published it in 1802); it was not formulated in 1870.
Graphically, it can be shown in Fig. 6.2.

blocks.alt: A graph of volume V against temperature T. A straight magenta line rises to the right; extended back to the left it meets the temperature axis at -273 °C, to the left of the vertical V axis.
blocks.caption: Figure 6.2: Charles' law shown graphically (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 6.2).

blocks.text: It is stated that for a fixed mass of an ideal gas, the pressure exerted by a gas varies directly with absolute temperature of the gas at constant volume.
Graphically, Gay-Lussac's law is shown in Fig. 6.3.

blocks.alt: A graph of pressure P against temperature T: a straight line rising from the origin.
blocks.caption: Figure 6.3: Gay-Lussac's law shown graphically (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 6.3).
